articles.title_orig: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.title_zh: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.content_orig:
While competition once centred on getting into college, teenagers are increasingly under pressure to get a higher secondary place
Moon Chen stared down at her textbook, struggling to make sense of the words on the page.
The 15-year-old felt a suffocating weight press into her chest, while her heart fluttered erratically.
Chen’s mother rushed her to a cardiologist – only to be told that she should see a psychiatrist instead.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israel’s president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Knesset has been deadlocked since the election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority
Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to ⁠try to ​form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man ⁠with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Netanyahu ‌is fighting to hold on to office ‌after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc ‌in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.
But it remains unclear if Eisenkot’s bloc would accept support from the Arab lists in forming a government.
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But the military man is no peacenik. He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.
Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo urges South America to bridge divides on Uruguay stop of 12-day tour
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo urges South America to bridge divides on Uruguay stop of 12-day tour
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff says he wants to bring a ‘message of hope’, as he returns to the continent that helped shape his priesthood
Pope Leo began an emotionally charged tour of South America on Friday, returning to a continent that helped shape his priesthood just three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old head of the Catholic Church will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru over 12 days in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades, meeting political leaders, prisoners, the poor, as well as old friends.
“I’m very happy to be here,” Leo told reporters on the plane before landing in Uruguay, saying he wanted to bring a “message of hope in today’s world”.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Believes Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: U.S. Believes Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Had a Relationship With a Suspected Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
He runs the most powerful A.I. company in the world, and now the U.S. government believes he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy: According to the Financial Times , U.S. officials believe that Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at the Nvidia customer Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence believes she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security. For Nvidia, worth more than $4 trillion on the stock market, the case has become a problem at the very top.
The report is based on a memo that U.S. officials wrote earlier this year, drawing on information obtained by American intelligence, the FT said. The memo said Mr. Huang had been romantically involved with Alice Huang. The two are not related. It was shared with a small group of top U.S. government officials shortly before President Trump traveled to Beijing in May for a summit with Xi Jinping. The White House and the C.I.A. declined to comment. Photographs and videos showing the two together have circulated on social media.
On Friday, The New York Times reported that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, worked directly for China’s top spy agency. Her tasks reportedly included persuading the Nvidia chief to lobby for exports of advanced chips to China. The operation dates back to at least 2024, according to The Times. In late October, the newspaper first reported that U.S. intelligence considered the Megaspeed executive a source for Beijing and that she had been in close contact with Jensen Huang .
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, was spun off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023. It is suspected of smuggling advanced Nvidia chips into China in violation of U.S. export controls. Nvidia conducted an internal review of the allegations and found no evidence of wrongdoing. The U.S. government has been investigating companies, particularly in Southeast Asia, that are believed to be funneling chips to China. Washington’s concern is that advanced A.I. chips could speed up China’s military modernization.
The case is all the more sensitive because Mr. Huang personally lobbied Mr. Trump earlier this year to let Nvidia sell its H200 chips in China . According to the FT, U.S. national security officials have privately expressed frustration with the Nvidia chief.
Mr. Huang has met with Mr. Trump several times since the president began his second term. An episode from May shows how close the two are: When Mr. Trump flew to China for the summit, Mr. Huang was not initially among the chief executives aboard Air Force One. When the president learned of this, he called Mr. Huang personally, according to the FT. The Nvidia chief then flew to Alaska and boarded the presidential plane during a stopover. In September, he attended the state dinner Mr. Trump held for Mr. Xi during his visit to the United States.
Now the case has reached Congress. Top Republican lawmakers have asked Mr. Huang to appear in private before the House committees on China, foreign affairs and intelligence. They want to ask him about the alleged spying operation and about Nvidia’s security protocols. According to The Times, a closed-door briefing is planned for mid-November.
Nothing has been proved so far, and all of the information comes from anonymous sources. Nvidia declined to comment on the memo or on the assertion that its chief executive had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang. The company has previously said that Mr. Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year.” John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesman, told The Times that the company does not share classified information with customers and that the interactions were “not unusual.” Alice Huang could not be reached for comment. The Chinese Embassy in Washington called the reports unsubstantiated and “nothing but smears against China.”

articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.content_orig:
The leader had offered to resign, but lawmakers went ahead with proceedings to strip him of immunity granted to former presidents
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena was placed under house arrest on Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.
Pena had offered his resignation over the disaster, but lawmakers pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings that would strip him of immunity granted to former presidents.
He did not attend the trial in the Senate despite earlier pledging to defend himself.

articles.title_orig: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.title_zh: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.content_orig:
Late night political drama as PeÃ±a is impeached and arrested
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.title_zh: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.content_orig:
A global review of commercial flight
SHANGHAI — GE Aerospace said November 6 that it had signed sales and service agreements worth more than US$12.9bn at the China International Import Expo, including engines and long-term support for China Eastern Airlines (MU).
Reuters reported the aggregate value and scope of the agreements , citing a GE Aerospace statement. The total covers multiple sales and service arrangements, rather than the price of China Eastern's new-aircraft engines alone.
China Eastern will purchase 202 LEAP-1A engines for 101 Airbus A320neo-family aircraft, Reuters reported. A separate agreement covers 14 spare engines across the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1C and CFM56-7B models. GE Aerospace also reached supply and repair agreements with MTU Maintenance Zhuhai, according to the report.
CFM International's November 6 announcement confirms China Eastern's engine selection for 101 aircraft, together with spare engines and a long-term services agreement. CFM is a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines.
The aircraft will include A320neo, A321neo and A321XLR models, CFM said, without providing an individual delivery schedule in its announcement. It says China Eastern already operates 215 A320neo and A321neo aircraft powered by LEAP-1A engines, making the selection an extension of an established engine fleet.
The airline also uses the LEAP-1B on Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and the LEAP-1C on COMAC C919s, according to CFM. These are distinct engine variants for different aircraft platforms; the spare-engine agreement spans both newer LEAP models and the older CFM56-7B.
MTU's Zhuhai facility description lists LEAP and CFM56 maintenance capabilities . Its separate Jinwan branch, operating since March 2025, focuses on Pratt & Whitney PW1100G-JM engines.
GE's latest financial results show the scale of the servicing opportunity. In its third-quarter results released October 20 , the company reported a commercial-services backlog exceeding US$170bn. Commercial Engines & Services revenue from services grew 17% year over year in the quarter; spare-parts revenue rose more than 20%.
CFM is also preparing for more LEAP maintenance as the installed fleet grows. Its July maintenance-network update described five-year investment commitments exceeding US$1bn by GE Aerospace and €1bn by Safran Aircraft Engines, alongside expansion of licensed maintenance providers and spare-parts inventories.
Those investments address the support needed after engines are delivered. For airlines, access to replacement engines, parts and repair slots can matter alongside the original purchase price. Airways has examined how engine-maintenance bills can remain elevated even as aircraft availability improves .
Neither CFM's announcement nor Reuters' account supplies a breakdown showing how the US$12.9bn total is divided between engine sales, spare engines and future maintenance.

articles.title_orig: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.title_zh: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.content_orig:
In the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction , as we noted in our previous sitrep, the situation has stabilized, and the advance of Russian assault troops around the town of Mykolaivka has effectively come to a halt. This is confirmed by new posts from the pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project, featuring geolocated footage of Russian strikes on Ukrainian positions in the villages of Piskunivka , Rai-Oleksandrivka , and Tykhonivka .
In the context of Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corpsâ use of ground robots equipped with grenade launchers was discussed . Now, footage has emerged showing a large-scale assault involving such robots, apparently in the Lyman direction , judging by the reference to the Russian Armed Forcesâ 3rd Motorized Rifle Division, which is part of the 20th Combined Arms Army. Pro-Russian sources report that 28 robots were destroyed by drones. On the one hand, launching such a large-scale robot assault without cover from friendly drones looks like a mistake. On the other, it may have been used as a diversion while assault infantry approached Russian positions along a different route.
The pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project has published its estimate of the Russian Armyâs advance in October, according to which the RuAF captured an additional 7.25 kmÂ² of territory. This is virtually zero compared with September, when the project recorded an advance of 177 kmÂ². We had expected that, if the trend observed in the first half of the month continued, the project would record a net loss of territory for the first time in several years of tracking. We do not know which territorial gains were included in the calculation to produce a positive figure.
Notably, these figures are close to the territorial gains by the AFU reported by Volodymyr Zelenskyy: 10.4 kmÂ² in October. At present, the Russian advance is approaching zero when the territorial gains of both sides are taken into account. Starting in November, the pace of offensive operations is expected to decline further with the onset of colder weather and the loss of foliage.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) reported on its Telegram channel that UAV operators of the Alpha Special Operations Center killed 2,146 Russian soldiers and wounded another 1,052 over the course of a week. This would amount to approximately 300 Russian soldiers killed per day, or more than 9,000 per month if extrapolated. This represents a substantial increase compared Ð° with figures reported in previous months: 6,000 âneutralizedâ in July and August , and 7,600 in September . The SBU claims that this particular unit leads the Ukrainian Defense Forces in the number of enemy targets struck.
Meanwhile, the Unmanned Systems Forces reported that their drones killed approximately 300 Russian soldiers per day in October, which would amount to another roughly 9,000 killed per month. This means that just two formations reportedly account for 18,000 Russian soldiers killed per month.
In our assessment, the RuAF's total irrecoverable losses (those killed in action, permanently disabled personnel, prisoners of war, and deserters) may amount to approximately 25,000-30,000 personnel per month. If the Unmanned Systems Forces and Alpha alone account for 18,000 KIA, less than half of Russia's total irrecoverable losses would be left to account for all other categories of irrecoverable losses and the results of operations by all other Ukrainian military branches, including artillery. If our estimate were incorrect and Russian losses actually reached nearly 50,000 per month, as claimed by various sources, the situation for the RuAF along the frontline would already be critical, as losses would significantly exceed recruitment levels (approximately 30,000 personnel per month). In that scenario, we would expect to see a genuine collapse of the frontline rather than the current situation, in which Ukrainian and Russian territorial advances are roughly comparable.
One argument supporting the credibility of Ukrainian figures on Russian losses is the e-points system and the verification of strikes through the Delta situational awareness system. However, we see no reason to assume that publicly released reports necessarily correspond to the actual statistics of units recorded in the internal system.
Michael Kofman is also skeptical of some Ukrainian public claims. In a podcast with a serviceman from the AFU's 3rd Corps, Kofman asked him not to cite an unrealistic casualty ratio between the two sides.
The Economist has estimated that between 374,000 and 770,000 Russian military personnel have been killed, with total casualties, including the wounded, estimated at between 1.4 million and 2.1 million. Many Russian-language media outlets ran headlines featuring only the upper bound, even though the difference between the upper and lower estimates exceeds the lower estimate itself, making it incorrect to present 770,000 as an established death toll. For comparison, by Oct. 30, BBC News Russian and the independent Russian media outlet Mediazona, together with volunteers, had established the names of 285,023 killed Russian soldiers. If we still assume that open sources account for 45-55% of deaths and that our previous formula works (though we no longer believe this to be the case), the actual number of Russian military personnel killed would be approximately 520,000. Due to high drone activity and an extremely low rate of advance, the recovery of bodies from the gray zone is difficult, and deaths are recorded in obituaries and government registries only after substantial delays. Therefore, a more complete picture of casualties for 2026 will likely emerge only in a year or two. The estimate of "around half a million killed" appears plausible, but the available data do not allow us to confirm or rule out The Economist's upper estimate of 770,000.
The humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky ended on the evening of Nov. 1. According to the latest figures , about 750 people were evacuated from the town (both sides decided not to disclose the exact number). Most of those who wanted to leave went to Ukraine, traveling by air from Anapa to Gomel and then by bus through Belarus. Some residents chose to go to Russian-controlled territory. Thousands of people remain in the town and its outskirts, so humanitarian missions need to continue.
The General Staff of the AFU and other Ukrainian military officials said Russian forces used the ceasefire to rotate personnel and bring up equipment and munitions. This does not, however, suggest that Russia is preparing an offensive against the city of Kherson : the Dnipro remains a formidable obstacle, and Russian troops cannot supply a large force on the river's right bank. Earlier, Sky News, citing Ukrainian marines, also reported ceasefire violations by the RuAF and published footage purportedly showing the violations. However, Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, did not confirm these allegations.
Yana Lantratova, the Russian Commissioner for Human Rights, said the Russian side is doing everything it can to help citizens and protect their rights. But Russia, as the occupying power, bears direct responsibility for protecting civilians who remain in Oleshky and for meeting their basic needs. Russian authorities could have evacuated residents from the dangerous area near the front line much earlier. The evacuation should continue even after the joint humanitarian operation has ended.
The US State Department has approved the sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles to Ukraine for $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected before 2030. To obtain the munitions sooner, Ukrainian officials are proposing that the United States and other partners transfer PAC-3 missiles from existing allied stockpiles and replenish them later with missiles produced under the new contract. Such an exchange is technically feasible, but it requires a political decision by the US administration

articles.title_orig: French far-left presidential hopeful pledges ‘revolutionary’ remaking of society
articles.title_zh: French far-left presidential hopeful pledges ‘revolutionary’ remaking of society
articles.content_orig:
Hard-left French leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has been described as a “radical” by right-wing opponents, a “despot” by former allies and a “hero” by some of the students who have taken to the streets in nationwide protests .
The leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party has emerged as the strongest contender on the left and potential challenger to far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential election.
On Saturday, Melenchon is presenting his programme at a rally in Le Bourget, north of Paris, a day after it was published online. Among his proposals, he wants to lower the retirement age to 60 and raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro ($1,900) a month; pull France out of NATO and renationalise parts of the economy.
He wants France to stop paying back the debt it owes to the European Central Bank, effectively transforming it into a permanent interest-free loan – a move he hopes would give the government more room to spend.
On Europe, he envisions France remaining in the EU, but he wants to refuse rules that conflict with the nation’s social, environmental or economic programmes, setting up a potentially confrontational relationship with Brussels.
His party is gaining momentum as protests led by students in mid-September swelled to include several groups angry about failing public services, rising living costs and uncertain futures. The hard-left leader has been hailed at marches, some of which have seen vandalism and looting.
“His strength is that he is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations: better wages, money in education, a lot of welfare measures, no austerity cuts which appease people who are fed up with the cost of living,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute. “He is the vote of the protesters.”
But some say his policies are radical and unrealistic.
France’s finances and borrowing are under scrutiny as its budget deficit and debt levels are high, raising further doubts on how Melenchon’s ambitious spending plans, particularly on social programmes and public investment, could be implemented. Some economists warn that his plans could cause investors to sell French government bonds, thereby increasing sovereign borrowing cost. “Borrowing money and deciding not to give it back – that’s called theft,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in September, regarding such proposals.
LFI says higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations – another pillar of Melenchon’s campaign – would finance its spending plans. His proposals include a minimum 2 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires, restoring France’s wealth tax and increasing taxes on large inheritances. “Financial capital has benefitted, and it is the one that should pay,” he said in October.
His programme draws on a tradition of left-wing economic interventionism, rooted partly in Keynesian thought, that argues that the state should play an active role in the economy to correct market’s imbalances.
“Because this tradition of state intervention in economic and social affairs has been abandoned by most other political parties, the fact that LFI continues to define itself through such interventionism creates an impression of radicalism,” said political analyst Beligh Nabli, a professor of public law at UPEC-Paris XII. “Yet, this radicalism is only relative – it appears radical when compared to other contemporary political offerings, but from the perspective of the history of social democracy, it is not radical at all.”
Melenchon, 75, was born in Morocco to French parents. He moved to France as a child where he later graduated in philosophy and modern literature. In the 1980s, he joined the Socialist Party, but distanced himself from it when it shifted towards more liberal economics.
In 2008, he finally quit the Socialists and founded the Left Party, which would later evolve into LFI. The party appealed to working-class voters and marginalised communities and became popular with young people. According to this week’s polls, the presidential candidate is polling between 17.5 to 18 percent, widening the gap with his rivals in the left camp.
Trailing behind is Raphael Glucksmann, who leads the centre-left Place Publique party and secured the backing of the Socialist Party after winning a joint primary in October. Further back, and running on their own ticket – the Communist Party’s Fabien Roussel, Marine Tondelier’s Greens party and independent Francois Ruffin.
The left-wing bloc is undecided on the LFI. As Melenchon holds a significant lead, smaller parties are weighing whether to support him to give a left-wing alliance a better shot. Glucksmann has ruled that out, but others are pondering the situation. “This will be one of the key debates throughout the presidential campaign,” said Nabil.
Another source of tension across the French left is Melenchon’s strong support of Palestine. He has repeatedly refused to describe Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a term other left-wing politicians, including Glucksmann, have been reluctant to use. Melenchon has also faced accusations from political opponents on the left that his rhetoric fuels anti-Semitism, claims he rejects.
But Melenchon’s popularity is nowhere close to that of National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen. The far-right leader, who challenged President Emmanuel Macron in a second round in the past two elections, would easily win in a run-off against Melenchon, leading 70 percent to 30 percent, according to a Toluna Harris Interactive poll conducted in October.
Analysts say his economic programme is not the only obstacle. His combative political style and reputation for confrontation over compromise hinder his chances of broadening support beyond a core base.
“In France, it is often said that to win a presidential election, one must campaign from the centre. Yet, the defining characteristic of the LFI programme is that it is not centrist – that is precisely what makes it disruptive. He seeks victory, but not a victory from the centre,” Nabli said.
His leadership has also been criticised.
Several former allies have said their break with the party was driven by both Melenchon’s management style and political disagreements. Former LFI candidate Thomas Guenole has described the movement as a “dictatorship” governed by “an autocrat”, while former lawmaker Raquel Garrido said there was a left that agreed with LFI’s programme but not with the party leader’s “methods”. Former close ally Clementine Autain has likewise accused LFI of becoming “authoritarian”.
“He is the ‘supreme leader’,” said Reland at the Global Policy Institute. “The party is very organised, but it’s not a democratic party at all.”

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.title_zh: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Meanwhile, Turkey's newly nominated Feridun Sinirlioğlu drew eight discouragement votes in his debut poll
Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Rebeca Grynspan, speaks during the opening ceremony of the 9th World Investment Forum (WIF 2026) in Doha, Qatar, on October 25, 2026.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan recorded another strong showing in the race for United Nations secretary-general on Thursday, increasing her support in the eighth Security Council straw poll, while Turkey’s newly nominated candidate struggled in his debut and the established front-runners maintained their positions.
Thursday’s straw poll again used undifferentiated ballots, concealing whether votes came from the five permanent, veto-wielding members — the U.S., United Kingdom, France, Russia and China — or the council’s 10 elected members. The selection process has also been shaped by informal regional rotation norms and calls for the U.N. to select its first female leader. The latest result shows that the newcomers took nothing from the front-runners, while Grynspan appears to be consolidating support.
Grynspan, a former Costa Rican vice president who would become the first woman and first Jewish person to lead the U.N. if selected, had her best day of the race, receiving 12 encouragement votes and three discouragement votes, according to reported results of the confidential ballot. Her showing improved from the previous round, when she received 11 encouragement votes and four discouragement votes.
However, the race is not yet settled as questions remain about whether she has overcome potential vetoes from permanent Security Council members. The last color-coded round, held Oct. 16, showed that Grynspan, International Atomic Agency head Rafael Grossi and Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett had each drawn two discouragement votes from permanent members. Grynspan has since lowered her total discouragement count from five to three, but the latest results do not clarify whether any opposing permanent members have changed their stance.
The results also suggest that the entry of two Middle Eastern candidates has done little to disrupt the established front-runners. Feridun Sinirlioğlu, a former Turkish foreign minister and U.N. ambassador nominated by Ankara last week, received just three encouragement votes and eight discouragement votes, with four members expressing no opinion.
Sinirlioğlu’s nomination added diplomatic nuance to the race, given President Donald Trump’s relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who remains highly critical of the Jewish state, and the administration’s efforts to defend Israel at the U.N. His initial straw poll preceded his scheduled town hall with the General Assembly on Friday and an informal dialogue with the Security Council on Monday.
Meanwhile, Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE’s former ambassador to the U.N., received seven encouragement votes, six discouragement votes and two “no opinion” votes — identical to her debut in the previous round.
Nusseibeh’s stagnant tally comes amid scrutiny over the UAE’s alleged support for the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group accused of committing atrocities in Sudan’s civil war. The UAE has denied providing military aid to the group. Nusseibeh has condemned RSF atrocities, expressed support for U.N. accountability efforts and stressed that she would serve independently of the Emirati government if selected.
The controversy has intensified following a New York Times report detailing findings from a confidential U.N. report concerning the UAE’s alleged role in recruiting and deploying Colombian mercenaries to support the RSF in Sudan’s civil war.
In addition, an investigation by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies found an online campaign opposing Nusseibeh’s candidacy had ties to individuals with Sudanese and Turkish interests, though it did not establish that either government directed the effort. It remains unclear how heavily the controversies have weighed on Security Council assessments.

articles.title_orig: Russia upgrades Abu Dhabi delegation as Zelenskyy warns Trump's plan is dangerous
articles.title_zh: Russia upgrades Abu Dhabi delegation as Zelenskyy warns Trump's plan is dangerous
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week.
Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down . In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.
"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."
"These negotiations are not the last," he said.
Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.
"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.
The meeting follows several weeks of strain in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship. In October, President Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to supply diesel to the United States for the first time since 2022. Elon Musk's SpaceX also imposed limits on Ukraine's Starshield satellite networks, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and some air-defense systems, before reinstating access weeks later.
Despite these developments, Budanov said he is optimistic about Ukraine's relationship with the United States heading into the trilateral meeting next week.
"Look, it's bad. It shouldn't be like that," Budanov said of the Starshield failures. "But along with that, we can remind you that this situation is resolved in one way or another. This gives optimism for the future."
The trilateral meeting comes as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Strikes this week hit energy facilities in 10 regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and cut water to much of Kyiv for more than 16 hours.
Budanov, speaking from his office in the capital, said Russia was using the strikes to create political pressure on Kyiv.
Russia's goal is "to cause the maximum damage to our critical infrastructure," he said. "What they hope to do is to create a foundation for social dissatisfaction, for street protests, and to stifle the national interests. But this will not happen."

articles.title_orig: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
articles.title_zh: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
articles.content_orig:
Eric Edmeades recalls how his father's assisted death came sooner than expected and explains why he believes Canada's MAiD program has gone "way past appropriate."
A Canadian man's decision to end his life through the country's medically assisted dying program left his son stunned by how quickly the process unfolded, and now he's warning that the system has gone "way past appropriate."
Eric Edmeades, founder of Speaker Nation, a training platform for speakers that teaches presentation skills and more, told Fox News Digital this week that his father Baz, who was in his late 70s and struggling with a combination of medical problems, began discussing Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) program after his health deteriorated in late 2023.
But what Edmeades expected to be a months-long process suddenly accelerated, leaving the family with little time to prepare.
I'M 25 WITH A TERMINAL DISEASE. WE NEED AN FDA COMMISSIONER THAT HEARS PEOPLE LIKE ME
Eric Edmeades with his father. (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said the family started taking the issue seriously in January, but at that stage, projections were that it would take at least six months. He and his wife traveled to Vancouver at the beginning of 2024 to visit his father. At that stage, it was still a speculative thing that was months away.
"And then all of a sudden it was like, ‘No, it's next week,’" Edmeades recalled.
His father died via MAiD on Feb. 27, 2024.
He had been experiencing a sharp decline in his physical health and independence, particularly during the COVID-era lockdowns, according to his son.
"He had been incredibly healthy most of his life," Edmeades said, describing a combination of symptoms that included epilepsy and neurological pain .
Edmeades also questioned whether interactions between his father's medications could have contributed to his deteriorating condition.
"When the lockdowns came along, and he could no longer go out and walk all the time, it really had a marked decrease in his physical ability and his sense of freedom and all that kind of stuff," he said.
"And then there just came this point where life started sounding pointless to him," Edmeades said.
CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH
Eric Edmeades with his father and family in Vancouver. (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said his father had previously spoken about suicide, making his initial interest in medically assisted dying less surprising to the family.
"Given that it wasn't the first time that he talked about suicide in his life, it wasn't particularly shocking, but he also wasn't talking about it in really alarmist terms. So, I wasn't overly worried about it," he said.
Edmeades and his wife had already planned a trip to Vancouver and were able to spend time with his father before his death.
"And one of the things I'm incredibly grateful for is that I had incidentally booked a trip out to Vancouver, and my wife and I got to spend time with him," Edmeades recalled.
He thought he and and his wife would have another opportunity to visit.
NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS
Eric Edmeades with his dad. (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said he was not in contact with his father's medical providers at the time and did not fully understand what had happened until afterward.
"It happened so quickly that I only really started to piece together what happened when it was done," he said.
Other family members and friends had also expressed concerns about his father's decision, according to Edmeades. He recalled that his brother openly opposed the decision and that one of his father's close friends spent approximately 45 minutes discussing the matter with him during his final days.
"At that stage, you know, for him, the decision was made," Edmeades said.
The experience has left Edmeades questioning whether Canada's assisted-dying program has adequate safeguards.
He acknowledged that there may be circumstances in which medically assisted dying is appropriate but argued that Canada's implementation has gone too far.
"What I see happening in Canada is way past appropriate," he said.
Edmeades also raised concerns about the government's role in overseeing the system, arguing that decisions about eligibility should be insulated from political influence and potential financial incentives.
"If I had to press a button and decide whether the MAiD program existed or didn't exist, I would say this," Edmeades said. "It should only ever exist if, and I mean if the process for approving people, it would be completely independent of government, and there could be no benefit to those people in making that preference in making that decision. Because otherwise there's a slippery slope, and we see that slippery slope."
According to the Government of Canada , individuals seeking medical assistance in dying (MAiD) must be at least 18 years old, capable of making their own medical decisions, and eligible for publicly funded healthcare. They must also voluntarily request the procedure without outside pressure and provide informed consent. To qualify, applicants must have a serious, incurable illness, disease or disability, be experiencing an advanced and irreversible decline in their abilities, and face persistent physical or psychological suffering they consider intolerable and that cannot be relieved in a way they find acceptable.
The government also announced legislation on Oct. 27, 2026, that would allow advance requests while preventing the planned expansion of MAiD eligibility to people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness.
According to the BBC , Canada’s MAiD law, which legalized euthanasia in 2016, is responsible for one in every 20 deaths in Canada.
NEW YORK NUNS WILL NOT BE FORCED TO COMPLY WITH ASSISTED-SUICIDE LAW WHILE CASE PROGRESSES
Canada’s MAID law legalized euthanasia in 2016. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
A report from the Canadian Medical Association Journal covered by EWTN News claimed that implementing assisted suicide will "save" the Canadian healthcare system between $34.7 and $136.8 million per year. The study noted that patients and physicians should not consider costs when making such grave decisions.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ian McLeod, senior advisor for media relations and Conseiller principal for the Department of Justice Canada, said, "Canadian law is extremely clear: medical assistance in dying (MAID) requires a voluntary request, freedom from external pressure, and the person’s informed consent, among other stringent eligibility criteria and safeguards. Knowingly failing to comply with these eligibility criteria and safeguards is a criminal offence."
McLeod continued, "In the current MAID structure found in Canada’s Criminal Code, the mental illness exclusion is meant to exclude eligibility for MAID on the basis of a mental illness, including suicidal ideation. The proposed amendment to the mental illness exclusion in Bill C-41, the proposed Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act, which was introduced on October 27, 2026, is meant to reinforce this."
McLeod added, "This is why the Bill reinforces that, in situations where a person has a mental illness and an eligible medical condition (e.g. physical or neurodegenerative illness), eligibility must be determined on the basis of the qualifying medical condition. A mental illness may contribute to a person’s suffering, but it cannot be the basis for determining that the MAID eligibility criteria are met. Importantly, having a mental illness does not, in itself, make a person ineligible for MAID."

Physician-assisted suicide is legal in 14 U.S. jurisdictions (13 states and Washington, D.C. (Thomas Jansen-Lonnquist for The Washington Post)

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.content_orig:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg , which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.

articles.title_orig: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.title_zh: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.content_orig:
Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient
I t was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.
Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.
But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.
Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.
This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.
Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign , which launched last month.
The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.
Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction .
The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War , distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.
For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.
It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.
The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.
But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.
This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.
Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.title_zh: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.content_orig:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

CAIRO -- Airstrikes in a town near the capital, Sanaa, on Saturday killed 22 people and wounded 30 others, mostly women and children, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said.
Speaking to The Associated Press, Anees Alasbahi accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the strikes in the village of al-Shariya. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The attacks came a day after Houthi officials said 30 people were killed in strikes on a market in southern Yemen. The Iranian-backed Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed military each blamed the other for that strike.

articles.title_orig: Man Under Investigation After Teen Rescued From Mountain
articles.title_zh: Man Under Investigation After Teen Rescued From Mountain
articles.content_orig:
Austrian police are investigating a German man aged 21 on suspicion of endangering public safety, after his 17-year-old female friend was left stranded on Germany's highest mountain Zugspitze in sub-zero temperatures.
The teenager called emergency services and was eventually rescued on the mountain at an altitude of about 2,500m (8,200ft).
She was suffering from hypothermia and taken to hospital in nearby Garmisch-Partenkirchen, over the border in Germany, before being discharged.
In Austria, anyone who endangers another person's physical safety can be punished with up to three months in prison.
The pair set off in the early hours of Sunday from the resort of Ehrwald in the Austrian Tyrol with the aim of seeing the sunrise on Zugspitze.
Temperatures that morning had fallen to -12C, a mountain rescuer told German Press Agency DPA.
The weather was so poor that the two climbers were soon knee-deep in snow, according to Austrian reports, and their plans to reach the 2,962m summit soon changed.
At one point they separated and the 21-year-old descended alone. The reason they split is unclear, and a police spokesperson declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.
Seven mountain rescuers responded to the call, and a helicopter eventually airlifted the teenager off the mountain. She was then taken to hospital by ambulance.
Although the teenager survived, what happened on Zugspitze on Sunday is reminiscent of a fatal incident on Austria's highest peak, the Grossglockner, in January 2025.
A 33-year-old woman froze to death on the Grossglockner after her boyfriend left her on the mountain, and he was later found guilty of grossly negligent manslaughter.
The boyfriend had insisted he had left her there while trying to get help, telling the court he had loved his girlfriend and that he was deeply sorry.
The case reverberated throughout the mountaineering community at the time, with prosecutors arguing that as the more experienced climber, he was the responsible guide on the trip and had failed to turn back or call for help in time.
In the latest case in Austria, police have said once they have completed their investigation, a report will be sent to Innsbruck public prosecutors, who will decide if a criminal offence has been committed.

articles.title_zh: Airline begins charging $140 for checked bags on some round-trip flights
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Planning to travel this Thanksgiving? Be prepared to fork over more cash for your checked bags.
Many airlines increased their checked bag fees back in March, following the outbreak of the war in Iran, when jet fuel prices skyrocketed. Now, JetBlue is doing it again.

With its latest round of price increases, you could pay up to $140 for a round-trip flight for a single bag. The fees, which are now in effect, apply to domestic flights, as well as flights to Canada, Latin America, the Caribbean and some Transatlantic destinations.
As airlines continue to struggle with higher operating expenses, we likely won't see the cost of travel come down any time soon.
JetBlue's new prices reflect peak and off-peak travel. So if you're traveling during Thanksgiving (Nov 19-30) or Christmas (Dec. 17 - Jan. 18), expect to pay more.
If you pay your checked-bag fee more than 24 hours in advance, it costs $50 for the first bag — that's up from the previous $39 — or $55 during peak travel for a one-way basic fare. If you pay less than 24 hours before you fly, then the cost is even higher: $60 (off-peak) and $70 (peak).
Checking a second bag? In advance, you'll pay $70 one way (off-peak) and $75 (peak). Less than 24 hours ahead of your flight, you'll pay $75 one way (off-peak) and $85 (peak). A third bag comes in at a flat $200.
It's gotten so complicated that there's a chart to consult , showing the checked-bag fees based on your fare class, origin, destination, travel dates and status with the airline.
But it boils down to this: A family of four checking one bag each at the airport over the holidays will pay $680 round-trip just for their bags. Once you add in seat selection, for-purchase meals and snacks and, in some cases, fuel surcharges, the cost of a trip might be more than you were budgeting for.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
The rising cost of jet fuel is just one of many factors impacting carriers' operating costs. That means, even if the price of jet fuel drops, airline travel isn't suddenly going to get cheaper.
"Pricing pressures are expected to ease gradually next year, but travel costs are unlikely to return to prior levels , as many of the forces driving higher prices have become long-term features of the industry rather than short-term disruptions," according to a statement by the Global Business Travel Association (GBTA).
While the cost of jet fuel is a significant factor in higher ticket fares, it's not the only one. GBTA also points to "structural factors including aircraft delivery delays, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) requirements, labor shortages and geopolitical uncertainty" as factors that will impact costs in the year to come.
JetBlue, for its part, reported a 21% jump in revenue during Q3, but still lost $257 million .
Back in March, JetBlue wasn't the only one raising fees. Other U.S. carriers, including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines all raised their checked-bag fees . In early May, low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines ceased operations altogether.
It's possible that other airlines will follow JetBlue's lead. But, even if they don't, the cost to check a bag remains high after the last round of increases in May: American Airlines charges $50 for your first checked bag and $60 for your second (you save $5 if you pay online). And Delta charges $45 for your first checked bag and $55 for your second.
However, fees vary by fare type, origin and destination. So if you're booking a flight, make sure to check the latest information on the airline's website.
The easiest way to avoid checked-bag fees is to avoid checking a bag altogether. But sometimes that's just not possible — say, if you're traveling during the holidays and have a suitcase full of gifts you're bringing with you.
If you plan on checking bags, you can save a bit of money by paying for them in advance. Or, you may be able to avoid those fees altogether with an airline-branded credit card.
There are several airline-branded credit cards that offer a free checked bag for the primary cardholder (and oftentimes a free checked bag for your travel companions). However, most cards that come with these types of perks also come with an annual fee, so if you're not a frequent flier, then the additional cost may not be worth it.
If you have a status in an airline loyalty program, then you may have perks like free checked bags. For example, JetBlue Mosaic 1 members receive one free checked bag, while members in higher tiers (Mosaic 2, 3 and 4) receive two.
Premium fares often come with free seat selection and checked bags, so it's worth comparing costs.
Keep in mind the lowest fare isn't necessarily the cheapest fare. Along with the base fare, also consider fees for seat selection and checked bags, which can quickly make a 'low' fare a lot more expensive.
