articles.title_zh: Democrats Just Swept Congress — and 80 Years of Stock Market History Says This Happens Next - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Eighty years of midterm history say stocks usually thrive after a divided Congress, yet Wall Street panicked within days. One crowded corner of the market could break a streak that has never failed, and three signals will show which way…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Voters handed Democrats both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms, so President Donald Trump will govern with a divided Congress starting in January 2027. Wall Street liked the result at first: the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year the next day. Then the mood turned. The tech-heavy index plunged 5.56% on November 5 as investors began pricing in tighter regulation of AI infrastructure . The VIX , Wall Street’s fear gauge, rose to 28.18 from 16.61 a session earlier.
That swing raises a question for investors. Eighty years of midterm history point to a good year ahead for stocks. This cycle could still test that record because so much of the market now rides on one theme.
The S&P 500 has risen in all 20 completed 12-month periods after midterm elections since 1946, gaining 14.7% on average. Divided government barely changes that. In 16 of the 21 midterms since 1946, voters sent the president a Congress controlled by the other party. The average 12-month return was 14.6% under divided government and 14.9% under unified government.
Today’s setup has the best record of all. The nine instances of a Democratic Congress combined with a Republican president produced an average S&P 500 gain of 16.2% over the following year. Gridlock means fewer policy shocks, a point Reuters reported traders were cheering right after the results.
AI-related companies now make up more than 30% of the S&P 500, and Democrats may push for tighter regulation of how much electricity and water data centers use. That pressure is building on its own. The Department of Energy projects data centers could account for up to 12% of U.S. electrical demand by 2028. PJM Interconnection’s independent market monitor called data center load growth “the primary reason” for tight supply and high capacity prices on its grid. Even without passing a law, a Congress with committee control can slow permitting through hearings alone.
Investors are already sorting winners from losers. From election day through November 6, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) fell 2.53% while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) slid just 0.94%. The tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) is down 13.41% over the past month.
Who controls Congress is just one factor among many. The economy grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter. The 10-year Treasury yield has fallen to 4.84% from 5.24% in early October, which helps growth-stock valuations. The Fed’s target rate is capped at 4.00%. Households are the weak spot: University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 48.1 in September, below the index’s recession threshold.
Keep the history in perspective. The samples are small, and returns ultimately come down to earnings, interest rates and valuations.

articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo
articles.title_zh: GTA 6's PS5 Physical Edition Revealed in First Photo
articles.content_orig:
Images of GTA 6’s physical edition have emerged on Reddit , ahead of its release later in the month.
The anticipated open world game – which won’t include a disc – looks practically identical to every other PS5 release, in a sealed blue plastic case with the usual logos and layout.
While this is a German copy, there’s a disclaimer on the front which mentions no disc is included, and only a download code is packaged inside.
The photos, first shared on Reddit but since deleted, have been reposted below:
Fans will be able to purchase boxed versions of the Rockstar release from retailers starting 12th November, allowing a week for them to pre-load the 212GB title ahead of launch .
This is the first major title to ship in a “code-in-box” format, although it will become a lot more common in 2028, when Sony’s signalled its intent to cease manufacturing Blu-ray discs .
Personally, I’m concerned about the waste of plastic here. I understand some people may still want a case to display with their other games, but if we’re getting rid of discs, I’d like Sony to implement some sort of recyclable format moving forward.
Remember, if you want a map of Leonidas to go with your physical copy of GTA 6, you’ll need to purchase that separately for $0.99 from the Rockstar Store.
You can find out more information about GTA 6’s pre-load through here .
In the meantime, do let me know if any of you are planning to purchase the physical version and why below.

articles.title_zh: Stellar Blade Nintendo Switch 2 tech analysis, including frame rate and resolution
articles.content_orig:
Stellar Blade came to Nintendo Switch 2 this week, and thanks to Digital Foundry, we have various technical details covering frame rate, resolution, and more.
Stellar Blade is one of the first games on the console to use frame generation, which is one of the things discussed here. We also have information about changes and cutbacks compared to the PS5 version.
Here’s the full roundup of tidbits:
– Switch 2 strips back environmental detail compared to PS5 – Pop-in is also more of a concern – In some shots, the cutbacks are less apparent – Details cut back more aggressively in larger scale shots – Lighting cutbacks as well – DLSS used on Switch 2 for a more stable presentation than PS5 – Switch 2 docked resolution is about 540p internally – Uses FSR3 frame generation by default on Switch 2 to take 30 FPS input to 60 FPS – Exploration usually better at hitting and holding 60 FPS for healthy periods – This isn’t done as often during combat and cutscenes with dropped frames – Extended dips don’t happen too often – With frame generation off, the game looks basically identical – With it off, internal docked resolution is about 648p – You’ll get a frame rate of about 35-45 FPS with it off – Handheld resolution is about 360p internally – Performance is similar with handheld and docked modes – In handheld mode with frame gen off, VRR helps with frame rate

articles.title_orig: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.title_zh: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
articles.content_orig:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen , a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence .
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz , a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal , a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron , a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson , a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

articles.title_orig: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.title_zh: Millions of ladders recalled nationwide after numerous reports of head injuries, skull fractures
articles.content_orig:
Apothecary Pharma recalls compounded tirzepatide vials distributed nationwide due to sterility concerns. Ashley Webster reports on the FDA classification of the recall and the North Carolina company's production practices.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is recalling more than 3.6 million Little Giant ladders after receiving dozens of reports of injuries, including head trauma and skull fractures.
The ladders, according to the recall , have a mechanism called "Rapid Locks" that are designed to be inserted into the ladders' rungs to help adjust the height.
According to a statement from Little Giant, the Rapid Locks can fail to become fully engaged, causing the ladders to retract and posing a potential fall hazard to consumers.
The company has received 25 reports of the ladders retracting, 19 of which resulted in injury.
NEARLY 6 MILLION COFFEE MAKERS SOLD AT MAJOR RETAILERS RECALLED OVER BURN RISK
Recalled Little Giant Adjustable Fortress 2.0 ladder (Unknown)
Those incidents resulted in three reports of head injuries which, according to the recall, include traumatic brain injury, skull fractures, concussions, vision loss, hearing loss and cognitive impairment.
The company has also received 16 reports of other injuries such as joint or bone fractures, lacerations and bruising.
Overall, the company has received 39 reports of the Rapid Locks not working properly.
WALMART RECALLS 4.4 MILLION GRILL BRUSHES OVER SERIOUS INJURY RISK
Recalled Little Giant Conquest 2.0 ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
The recall involves 11 makes of Little Giant's ladders and over 130 models ranging from $100 to $1,000.
Little Giant is adding supplemental warning labels to affected ladders, instructing users to visually verify that all Rapid Locks are fully engaged before climbing.
"You should stop using your ladder until you have received and applied the warning labels included in the repair kit according to the enclosed instructions, which contain further guidance on safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," Little Giant said in a statement announcing the recall.
The company is also sending repair kits to all known users with Rapid Locks malfunctions.
"The repair kit contains instructions, also accessible via the QR code on the ladder, for safely operating the Rapid Locks and maintaining the Rapid Locks with lubrication," the company added.
Recalled Little Giant Quantum ladder (U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission / Unknown)
CPSC advised consumers to maintain the Little Giant ladders' Rapid Locks with lubrication and to evaluate their ladders on a regular basis.
"If a lock does not function properly after this evaluation, the company will offer the choice of a replacement ladder of the same or equivalent model or a refund ranging from a depreciated value determined by date of purchase up to full purchase price for ladders purchased within the past 12 months," CPSC said in the recall.

articles.title_orig: America's newest small business owners with no employees are off to a hot start in AI era
articles.title_zh: America's newest small business owners with no employees are off to a hot start in AI era
articles.content_orig:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
My first official role in AI was at Facebook. I started as an intern and then joined full-time in 2018. I worked on AI research and development for the ads system that's powered by AI.
I don't have an engineering degree or background; I studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin. Part of why I think I got my role at Facebook was because I spent time building my own side projects and teaching myself how to train AI models and do data analysis.
I left Facebook in 2020 to start my own business in the wine industry, and after that company sold, I founded an AI company. I would need to double the number of people on my team if we didn't use AI playbooks.
If you're being thoughtful about setting up your AI operations, it's no different than building a team that you can trust.
That's something a lot of people are missing: how to actually make these systems things you can take your eyes off and not keep yourself up at night in the process.
My first business was a photography business, and I was too young to even drive to meet my clients. I would always catch rides with people, and my parents hated this.
I got into tech because in college, I was exposed to colleagues doing data analytics and working with coding and AI at summer internships. That led me to look online and try to take related classes, and I started to see that if you break a business problem into small enough pieces, you can get AI to handle parts of it: predicting, sorting, generating.
Later, when I was applying to Facebook , I used AI and data analysis to build a report of coffee shops in Austin that were less likely to be too busy for me to study at. I think that project helped me land my role.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
After I left Facebook , I started a wine business called Vinebase in 2020; we built a tech platform that used AI to help winemakers sell their wine online and manage the digital side of their business.
Because this was before AI became more mainstream, we didn't market it as AI. We called it our "auto magic" system. I think that if we had said it was AI, it could've been a turnoff for our customers. Vinebase was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022.
My sister and I started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022, because I was using AI in Vinebase and saw how the technology was progressing. ChatGPT came out about a month later and started really accelerating the AI timeline, so we went all in.
We have four full-time employees and four part-time contractors right now, but we'd need double if we weren't running as much as we are on AI. Given the company's current size, we'd need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, customer support specialist, executive assistant , and operations coordinator.
The way we structure these systems is based on something we call playbooking. Every department in the company has its own system. Each system is a collection of playbooks with AI agents that can run independently or together.
To build an AI playbook, pick one piece of work you do over and over, and write down what starts it, what goes into the task, and what should come out at the end. Next, write the steps the way you'd train a new hire: each step, the decisions in it, and what "good" looks like.
Start running it with AI, and while you watch, compare the result to how you would've done it. Then, fix the playbook, not the output, until you trust it to run without you.
I always think through how I want a playbook to work and outline it by hand. Whenever you're making an AI playbook, you want to own the thinking and the logic. Otherwise, you can fall into the trap of including something that you don't really understand, and then you're not going to be able to trust that system anyway.
We have an AI agent running our sales playbook to review customer calls and ensure they meet our standards, rather than having a sales manager review them manually. Also, instead of sales team members needing to ask their manager questions, they just ask the playbook, which then pulls the answers from our guide for that team.
There are two types of AI costs we have in the business. The first is the subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT for every person on the team. The other is because the majority of our operations are these AI playbooks that are running in the background without us being the ones starting or triggering it. In September, we spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run our playbooks in the background, which is billed by usage and is separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscription costs.
We say "own the playbook, rent the tech," which means that if you are creating really good playbooks for your AI to follow, it actually doesn't matter which tool you're running it in.
Right now, we have a setup that's running with Claude Code in the background. But I could run all of these playbooks in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot .
We try to avoid a lot of the risks that people are concerned about with AI going rogue by creating these detailed outlines. We don't just want the agents to run on vibes. There still needs to be a person to decide and design how the work gets done; AI just speeds up everything else. That's the job security we have in this AI era.
A few of us on the team who are more advanced with AI own the bigger, team-wide playbooks that the business depends on, but everyone playbooks their own personal workflow, and then we use that as the testing ground to graduate things into becoming more part of official systems.
My advice would be to just start with something small and really easy, because once you get your first win and see how AI can do that repetitive work for you, it's kind of like a snowball.
Do you have a story to share about using AI to run your small team? Contact this editor, Agnes Applegate, at aapplegate@businessinsider.com .

articles.title_orig: Why Italy’s Giorgia Meloni Is Willing to Lose Votes Over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Why Italy’s Giorgia Meloni Is Willing to Lose Votes Over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Giorgia Meloni wants EU leaders to decide who can speak for them in Ukraine peace talks. Her letter to António Costa reflects a position she took before entering office: Ukraine’s right to defend its independence matters to Italy’s own security, even when defending it costs her votes.
On Nov. 5, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni asked European Council President António Costa a question the European Union has left unanswered for far too long. Who has the authority to speak for the EU in negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine?
In her letter to Costa , Meloni pointed to a series of uncoordinated diplomatic initiatives, including individual European leaders holding talks with Vladimir Putin. She called for a decision at the December summit and made clear that she was seeking the role neither for herself nor for Italy. At a time when Moscow is counting on European divisions, the prime minister of one of the EU’s largest countries has asked her fellow leaders to agree on who speaks for them.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Four years ago, many expected Meloni herself to be the source of just such a division. Her party had roots in Italy’s post-fascist tradition, and her coalition partners gave her critics plenty of ammunition. Silvio Berlusconi spoke openly about his friendship with Putin. Matteo Salvini had spent years expressing sympathy for the Kremlin. The expectation was that, under Meloni, Italy would become the West’s weak link on Ukraine.
Meloni made her position clear before she even entered office. When Berlusconi sought to excuse Moscow’s invasion and attacked Volodymyr Zelensky in the autumn of 2022, she told him there would be no place in her government for parties that rejected Italy’s European and Atlantic commitments. She needed Berlusconi to form a coalition. Yet she chose Russia and Ukraine as the issue on which she would not compromise.
In doing so, Meloni posed a question to Europe’s right that many of its politicians would still prefer to avoid. If patriotism rests on a people’s right to determine its own future, what could be more patriotic than Ukraine’s resistance to Russian occupation? No one can credibly defend the sovereignty of their own country while accepting Russia’s supposed right to dictate a neighboring nation’s borders and government by force. Yet some European nationalists try to reconcile those positions by treating Moscow’s territorial demands as the basis for peace.
At the Crimea Platform summit on Aug. 23, 2023, Meloni reminded her audience that Russia’s aggression had begun in 2014, with the seizure of Crimea and the occupation of parts of the Donbas. She also acknowledged that Western governments had been wrong to assume Putin would stop there. After Crimea, major business deals continued, energy ties endured and diplomats tried to bring relations with Moscow back within acceptable bounds. Putin drew the lesson that military conquest could become an accepted political fact. Ukraine was left to live with the consequences.
“Your freedom is freedom for the whole of Europe,” Meloni told Ukrainians that day .
That argument has particular force for Italy. If Russia can force Ukraine to surrender territory and accept limits on its independence, the next European country it threatens will face a Kremlin with good reason to believe that aggression pays. Should that country be a NATO member, Italy and its allies would face a choice between a military response and abandoning their commitment to collective defense. Either would carry a grave cost. It is far wiser to prevent that dilemma while Ukrainians are still fighting the aggressor themselves.
Meloni is prepared to make that case to Italian voters. In September, she told Il Foglio that, in purely electoral terms, it would have been easier not to support Ukraine. Ahead of next year’s election, she ruled out an alliance with parties that vote against military aid for Kyiv .
Salvini opposes further arms deliveries, and some voters on the right want closer ties with Moscow and an end to sanctions. Every new package for Kyiv gives Meloni’s coalition partners an opportunity to reopen the argument. She has had ample opportunity to scale back assistance and spare herself the confrontation.
Instead, her government is preparing a 13th military assistance package for Kyiv . Italy has already supplied air defense equipment, and Defense Minister Guido Crosetto has said he will seek to extend the aid arrangements into 2027 despite opposition within the coalition. In 2025, Rome also hosted the Ukraine Recovery Conference , bringing governments, financial institutions and businesses together to plan for Ukraine’s reconstruction.
Putin’s strategy toward the West depends in part on the expectation that elections will eventually deliver what his army cannot. He has every interest in Italian politicians turning each shipment of air defense equipment into an argument about what it might cost them at the polls. Ukrainian families, meanwhile, are raising children for whom air-raid sirens are part of ordinary life. They know precisely what a shortage of air defenses can cost.
On Oct. 14, that same understanding of Italy’s interests put Meloni at odds with Donald Trump. Speaking in the Italian parliament, she called his agreement with Russia on diesel supplies a very risky decision. She warned that the deal could give Moscow additional revenue to finance its war, weaken sanctions and lend Russia legitimacy while Russian bombs continued to fall on Ukrainian cities.
Meloni shares much of Trump’s conservative outlook and has invested in good relations with his administration. That is what gave her criticism weight. Relations with the United States are a cornerstone of European security. But a European leader who believes an American decision will help sustain Russia’s war economy ought to be able to say so in public. Meloni did.
Her letter to Costa brings the argument back to Europe. Individual leaders can hold talks with Putin, but who gave any one of them a mandate to speak for the other member states? Meloni wants the EU to agree on a representative at its December summit and to coordinate with Britain, Norway and other partners. Costa has agreed to raise the issue with EU leaders . By declining to put herself forward, Meloni has left her colleagues to answer the question on its merits. If they want Europe’s interests represented in negotiations, they must decide who has the authority to represent them.
In 2022, many judged Meloni by her party’s origins and her coalition partners’ ties to Moscow. Four years later, they can judge her by her decisions. She drew a line with Berlusconi when she needed his support to take office. She challenged Trump over a deal she believed would help finance Russia’s war. And she has told her own voters why defending Ukraine matters to Italy, even if some of them vote against her for it.
Those who casually dismissed Meloni as just another European populist owe the public an honest admission that they were wrong. As for her fellow European leaders, they might recall what she told Ukrainians in 2023. If Ukrainian freedom is the freedom of all Europe, surely it is worth risking an election for.
Dr. Orhan Dragaš is a Serbian expert on security and international relations. He is the founder and director of the International Security Institute, based in Belgrade; author of numerous expert articles, newspaper columns, as well as the books "The modern intelligence-security community, utopia or reality"; and; "Two faces of globalization – truth and deceptions."

articles.title_orig: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.title_zh: An Update On A Possible ‘GTA 6’ PC Release Date Plans, Due To AI
articles.content_orig:
Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU , we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.
The rise of AI-powered reverse-engineering tools —which can quickly turn a console game binary into easy-to-port raw code with incredible brute-force efficiency and minimal human effort—might change that kind of “PC can wait” calculus for Rockstar. “I think I would be concerned, if I was Rockstar, that somebody would just take the PS5 version and get AI to change it to PC,” Vermeij told Rock Paper Shotgun.
To be sure, decompiling a game as complex as Grand Theft Auto VI wouldn’t be as simple as, say, the previous human-led decompilations of early 3D GTA games . But even if an AI coding harness has some difficulty capturing all the details of GTA VI ‘s advanced weather systems and scripted sweat simulations , that doesn’t mean it’s impossible.
Vermeij speculated that reverse-engineering the console version of GTA VI could cost “tens of thousands of dollars in tokens,” and a resulting port probably “won’t be as good as [Rockstar’s] effort” in the end. That said, Vermeij said it would probably be good enough to satisfy some potential PC players and that he “wouldn’t be surprised if there was an effort to get [the releases] a little bit closer together” to get ahead of that.
“What was the case before is that there’s so much effort in developing the game, that it is not possible to rip it off, and that’s completely changed now,” Vermeij said. “So, yeah, we’re going to have to see in the next couple of years how that’s going to pan out.”
While there hasn’t been an official timing announcement for the PC port of Grand Theft Auto VI , reports suggest Rockstar is currently aiming for the first quarter of 2027.

articles.title_orig: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.title_zh: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.content_orig:
When Carter Stevens tells people he makes six figures a year digging through dumpsters, they often assume he's "blowing smoke," he says.
Not everyone sees dollar signs in a brimming dumpster. But Stevens earned roughly $140,000 in total sales between September 2025 and September 2026 by salvaging trashed items, cleaning them up and selling them on platforms like eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It.
Stevens primarily operates near office parks and luxury condominiums around Nashville, Tennessee. Since March 2024, when he started dumpster diving, he's found and sold hand-crafted Persian rugs, high-end office chairs and even samurai swords, he says. Trash-picking helps him keep his shipping costs low, he adds: Some of his supplies, like cardboard boxes and packing tape, also come from dumpsters, enough that he doesn't have to pay for them approximately "90% of the time."
"The amount of waste in this country that you'll find is unbelievable. We throw so much stuff out," says Stevens, 31.
Sometimes, Stevens asks a building for permission to go through its trash, marketing himself as a junk removal service. In that way, his job is similar — though not identical, because he generally only takes what he can sell, he says — to other entrepreneurs across the U.S. who follow advice in Reddit threads or YouTube tutorials to launch junk removal side hustles or full-time businesses . There are around 10,000 junk removal businesses across the U.S., according to the Better Business Bureau. They range in scale from independent side hustles to national companies like 1-800-GOT-JUNK , which touts more than 150 franchise locations.
Other times, Stevens finds himself neck deep in rubbish, ducking concerned security guards, peeling away actual trash and rotting food in the hope of uncovering discarded treasure, he says. He tries to avoid sneaking around and keeps an eye out for "no trespassing" signs. He'd rather leave items behind if a property owner or security guard tells him to vacate the premises, he says.
Even Stevens expresses surprise at how much money he's made, saying he doesn't necessarily think his annual income is sustainable. When he "stumbled into" dumpster diving, he was approximately $12,000 in debt after years of poor spending habits fueled partially by a drug addiction, a stark change from his affluent childhood, he says.
"I dug myself out of a hole. I built up my savings. I really did much more than I thought was possible," says Stevens.
Stevens, a Nashville native, is the son of a five-time Grammy Award-winning producer of country and gospel music who has worked with artists like Blake Shelton and Carrie Underwood. His life took a turn in college when he developed an addiction to prescription Adderall, leading him to drop out partway through his senior year in 2018, he says.
His lack of a college degree made landing full-time work a challenge. He says his parents can afford to support him financially, and they've done so in specific emergency occasions. But mostly, his father wants his kids to learn to fend for themselves, he says: "He will let me sit on the coals for the sake of learning how to swim. That's taught me a lot [and] given me a lot of valuable skills and a tough mentality."
Unemployed, Stevens started combing through thrift shops and Goodwill clothing racks for vintage apparel to sell on eBay. He was inspired by YouTube influencers like Rick Senko, he says, whose Fort Lauderdale, Florida-based clothing resale business Technsports brought in $6.5 million in annual revenue as recently as 2024.
But Stevens' returns were inconsistent, and he often spent his profits on drugs or luxury shopping sprees, he says. After his parents funded a rehab stint in 2021 — helping him "quit doing the hard drugs," he says — he spent his money chasing other dopamine hits. Those indulgences included a $1,200 pair of Christian Dior Birkenstock sandals, an 85-inch flat-screen television and a $30,000 down payment on a Mercedes-AMG sedan that he later lost because he couldn't afford the total cost, he says.
By June 2023, he could no longer afford to pay rent, so he lived in a rented storage unit until the business's security found and evicted him, and then stayed in his Nissan Sentra for three weeks, he says. Homelessness shocked him into learning to manage his "reckless" spending habits, he says: "Being punished by your own spending addiction was a wringer that I promised myself I can't be put through again."
In October 2023, a cousin lent him money to start renting an apartment, and Stevens worked to stick to a sensible enough budget for his thrifting income to cover future rent and basic expenses, he says. Five months later, he found a discarded pair of black Nike Air Force Ones in good condition next to a gas station pump. He took them home, sanitized them and sold them online for $35, he says.
"That was the first time I had ever found something that was trash and sold it and made a little bit of money," says Stevens.
Once he started dumpster diving, Stevens was hooked "because I never stopped finding good stuff in these dumpsters," he says.
His biggest score to date: dozens of discarded Steelcase office chairs, worth $1,000-plus each when new, outside an overflowing office park dumpster, he says. He got his car — by this point, a used pickup truck and a self-built trailer — and hauled away 190 chairs to list online at hundreds of dollars apiece. He sold the majority of them in bulk transactions on Facebook Marketplace for $17,000, and brought in an additional $10,600 selling the remaining chairs individually, documents show.
If Stevens manages to find roughly one valuable haul per month, he can fill his $400-a-month storage unit and start listing the items. For the most part, he scopes out corporate environments, preferring "dry dumpsters" over ones laden with food waste, he says. Office trash is particularly profitable when companies downsize, says Stevens: Once, he found 120 standing desks discarded outside a building.
Near high-end apartment buildings, Stevens has found furniture from brands like West Elm, iPads, electronics and power tools in working condition, he says. "Almost every piece of furniture in my apartment came from a dumpster," says Stevens.
Stevens works alone and minimizes gas costs by sticking to locations within a few miles from his apartment. The majority of his income has come from big hauls across his five highest-earning months, reflecting the venture's hit-or-miss nature. "I got really lucky earlier this year and I made a ton of money. I'm not acting like this is something I could do every year," he says.
So he saves as much of his earnings as possible, "constantly" talking himself out of unnecessary purchases, he says. And he's studying the business of real estate wholesaling — which involves securing contracts for distressed properties and flipping them to investors for a fee — as a potentially more secure way to earn a living, he adds.
Still, he acknowledges the allure of knowing his next big payday could always be one dumpster away.
"I don't see myself ever turning down a good looking dumpster," says Stevens. "I have found so much cool stuff that I feel like I'll always be curious about what's in that dumpster."

articles.title_orig: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
articles.title_zh: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
articles.content_orig:
MILAN — Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said Saturday that his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, an encrypted part of the internet, and that he has been exposed to “threats and intimidation.” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russian hackers for the leak.
Tajani made the announcement in a social media post following a string of hoax bomb threats across Europe that caused flight diversions, security threats against broadcasters as well as recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
“For days, cybercriminals have been spreading my personal data on the dark web and seeking other information, in fact exposing me and my family to new threats and intimidation,” Tajani said, adding that the criminals “are prepared to pay for other details on me and my loved ones.”
Meloni, in a separate statement, expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data.” She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination.”
Tajani, who is also a vice premier in Italy’s government, did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.
“I will not allow myself to be intimidated in any way,” Tajani said. “I will continue working to defend my ministry, and Italy, and I will further strengthen the ties and cooperation to protect ourselves together.”
Tajani did not indicate who might be responsible for the cyberattack but reiterated the Italian government’s support for Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: 'Horrible' Mass Stranding in NZ Leaves Dozens of Dead Whales
articles.title_zh: 'Horrible' Mass Stranding in NZ Leaves Dozens of Dead Whales
articles.content_orig:
Rescuers were unable to save the whales after they became beached on a remote and rocky part of the country
More than 40 pilot whales died after a mass stranding event on New Zealand’s remote east coast, conservation officials said on Friday, despite rescue efforts by volunteers and conservation workers.
The Department of Conservation (DoC) said 43 whales had died in the mass stranding along the Ngawi coast on the south-eastern tip of the North Island.
The whales were reported to DoC just after 8am on Thursday, after which conservation staff, Maori iwi, or tribe, and volunteers tried to save them. However, “none of these whales are believed to have survived,” said Ariana Hawira, acting operations manager for DOC Wairarapa.
After the whales were first spotted trapped among the rocks, rescuers attempted to refloat some of the surviving animals, but they were largely unsuccessful.
Efforts to save the whales were hampered by the remote location, powerful surf, and sharp rocks in the intertidal zone, said Project Jonah, a group that was involved in the rescue attempts.
“When the whales were discovered, an estimated 40–50 whales were stranded along several kilometres of coastline,” Project Jonah said in a Facebook post on Friday. “Many had already died before they were found and sadly the whales that were found alive, succumbed throughout the day.”
The conservation department is working with iwi to manage the burial of whales, Hawira said. Whales are considered a taonga – a sacred treasure – by Māori.
Whale strandings are fairly common in New Zealand and more than 5,000 strandings of whales and dolphins have been recorded since 1840, according to DOC.
Pilot whales are a member of the dolphin family and can grow up to seven metres (23 ft) long and weigh up to 3 tonnes. The species are prolific stranders, although the behaviour is not well understood, Hawira said.
“While stranding on this part of the coastline is uncommon, there does not appear to be any indication of strandings becoming more frequent or severe,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Strategists Call Stock Rout a Fresh Reason to Buy
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Strategists Call Stock Rout a Fresh Reason to Buy
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off .
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire more than doubled its share repurchases last quarter to $9.6 billion, while operating earnings declined slightly, the company said on Saturday .
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite , which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a " correction ," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday .
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a " significant opportunity " ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet , saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and " we saw Google as a significant player . "
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett .
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion , falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's , however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses ," Chevron , and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon , HP , Paramount (now Skydance) , General Motors , Constellation Brands , and Pool .
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion . The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports , Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."

articles.title_orig: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.title_zh: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
articles.content_orig:
By Derek Gatopoulos, Dmytro Zhyhinas and Dan Bashakov | Associated Press
KYIV, Ukraine — Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war . The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv , damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.
“The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It’s very hard. No sleep, no peace — nothing. The children aren’t sleeping, and neither are we,” she told The Associated Press. “I’m old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?”
Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv’s 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city’s Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city’s energy situation as “extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.”
In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by “launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.”
Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression,” he wrote in an online post.
The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.
Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.
The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.
“When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv — a city of millions — and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone,” Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry said Saturday’s missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.
The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha , devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.
Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.
“She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?” he said. “She didn’t come home, and they didn’t find her body there. She isn’t in the morgue, and she isn’t here alive.”
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.
The head of Russia’s southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged “civilian infrastructure” and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.
The head of Russia’s Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.
Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol’s Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.
Vasilisa Stepanenko in Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, and Katie Marie Davies in Manchester, England, contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Strait of Hormuz could reopen under Qatari plan to end US war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Qatar has floated a new plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict between the United States and Iran, despite reports of renewed US strikes on a key Iranian island .
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of mediating Qatar, spoke with US president Donald Trump about their vision for a deal to end the eight-month war, Qatari media reported on Friday.
Al-Thani said on Saturday that the Trump administration was willing to find a solution after the midterm elections, which produced a damning verdict of the conflict and its impact on fuel prices last week.
Under Qatar’s proposal, the US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports and release some of its £6bn worth of frozen Iranian assets, according to the Guardian .
Iran would also agree to visits by IAEA nuclear watchdog inspectors to its main facilities, before reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic on the second day, the newspaper said.
Under the Qatari deal, and crucially for Trump, who casus belli was that Iran should never be able to acquire nuclear weapons, the regime would apparently not have to give up its nuclear stockpiles.
The Islamic Republic has made overtures to controlling the vital Strait, through which around a fifth of global oil normally passes, with Oman after the war and could begin charging fees for safe passage.
Under the Qatari deal, Tehran would reopen the route already agreed with Muscat, to be jointly lodged with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, has separately spoken with Iran about the future administration of the Strait, including the need to register the proposal with the IMO.
Muscat has its own long-term proposal for the running of the channel, which would only see shipping companies charged for services, not tolls per se.
Iran has also sought to resolve a number of secondary issues thrown by the conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
Ending the parallel clashes in Lebanon, pulling US forces back from the region and paying war reparations are all new obstacles that will require mediation.
Tehran has been proposing its own seven-day plan to end the war since September, but that has so far been rejected by Trump.
It calls for Washington to lift its blockade, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, after which the contested waterway would be reopened.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran has also submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar.
They said the US was reviewing its but that future discussions would still depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven stated demands.
Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy head of Iran's top security body, told Iranian state television on Friday that they were still not satisfied with “paper commitments” and must see practical steps from the US.
With diplomatic efforts still on ice, Iranian media on Saturday said it appeared two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to new attacks by striking at US and Israeli targets in neighboring countries.
The United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic couldn’t have picked a worse time to pull off the biggest IPO the world has ever seen.
Thursday marked one of the sharpest sell-offs on Wall Street in years. Tech stocks bore the brunt, but almost no equities were spared as fears of an AI slowdown gripped investors and sent them rushing to safety. The Nasdaq Composite lost $2.5 trillion in value , the biggest single-day dollar-value drop in its history. Asian and European markets followed the US down on Friday.
Put simply: The vibes around AI have never been worse, and Anthropic — a company that seldom misses a chance to warn of doomsday scenarios — is trying to convince investors the future for AI has never been brighter.
Thursday’s losses were so severe, some market commentators speculated that the company — which has been expected to make history this month with a target valuation of around $1.5 trillion — may have to delay the deal or significantly lower its price.
Before Tuesday’s midterm elections, traders on the prediction market Kalshi had put the likelihood of Anthropic’s IPO taking place this month above 90% But on Thursday, as markets tumbled over fears the Democratic sweep would throttle the AI buildout, those odds fell to 60%.
Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment.
“My view is that Anthropic can still come to market and will come to market [but] will likely be forced to do so at a lower valuation,” Mike O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, told CNN in an email.
The market rout comes just days before Anthropic was expected to begin its pre-IPO “roadshow,” a process in which private companies try to stir up investor interest and gauge demand before pricing its shares.
The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that three “major investors” who plan to participate in the IPO said the valuation would need to come down from the $1.5 trillion level analysts and investors have forecast.
Investors have been awaiting Anthropic’s IPO in part because it is expected to serve as a barometer for not only the AI trade but the broader US economy, which has been buoyed by heavy investment in the data centers and energy infrastructure that Anthropic’s technology requires.
At the same time, public sentiment around AI has been souring. Wall Street has been questioning whether companies may be overestimating the amount of demand they’ll see in the near future for AI.  All of that was already weighing on AI-related stocks in the lead-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections. Markets rallied to historic highs on Wednesday after Democrats’ decisive win, followed by President Donald Trump’s comments that he would work with the opposition.
But by Thursday, the reality of that Democratic sweep’s impact on AI settled in. Voters overwhelmingly elected candidates who are critical of data-center development — one of many potential pitfalls Anthropic warned about in its IPO prospectus last month.
Even Dan Ives, one of the most bullish AI voices on Wall Street, struck a subdued note in an email to clients Thursday, saying he now expects the breakneck growth of Big Tech companies’ spending on AI to peak in 2027 rather than 2028 or 2029.
“Our overall bullish tech thesis around the AI Revolution does not change, but it makes us more selective in the names and sectors that will outperform into 2027.”
The political shift compounds an already complex financial picture for Anthropic. The AI company this week disclosed in an updated regulatory filing that it has committed to spending nearly $900 billion in the coming years on computing power and data centers — a staggering amount relative to the $132 billion in cash and investments the company was sitting on a month ago.
“Many assumed the push for data center moratoriums was political theater that would fade after the election,” O’Rourke said in a note to clients Thursday. “This is no longer a bull-bear debate on AI infrastructure demand, there is clear evidence that a structural shift in the environment is underway.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.
